questions.prompt: Why does Part 2 begin with continuous performance management and CFRs?
choices: Because OKRs work better inside a broader ongoing system of conversation, feedback, and recognition
Because stretch no longer matters after Chapter 14
Because the book is leaving goals behind entirely

explanation.gentle: The chapter opens Part 2 by widening from goals into the larger system that supports them.
explanation.direct: Its job is to show that OKRs work best inside continuous performance management and CFRs.
explanation.competitive: The goal logic now needs the operating system that can carry it.

questions.prompt: What are CFRs in this chapter?
choices: Conversation, feedback, and recognition
Comfort, focus, and reach
Coaching, forecasting, and rating

explanation.gentle: The chapter introduces CFRs as conversation, feedback, and recognition.
explanation.direct: These are the core support practices paired with OKRs in Part 2.
explanation.competitive: The system needs more than goals. It needs live human signals around them.

questions.prompt: How does the chapter distinguish continuous performance management from annual-review logic?
choices: Continuous management relies on ongoing support rather than waiting for a static periodic judgment alone
Continuous management removes all accountability
Continuous management only means more frequent scoring

explanation.gentle: The chapter values support that happens while the work is still alive.
explanation.direct: Ongoing conversation and feedback are stronger than delayed judgment alone.
explanation.competitive: A yearly snapshot is softer than a live system.

questions.prompt: Lena works in a team where useful feedback arrives mostly at one big yearly review. What best fits the chapter?
choices: The chapter would treat this as weaker than ongoing conversation and feedback
The chapter would treat yearly review as enough because it is formal
The chapter says feedback should be minimized to avoid pressure

explanation.gentle: The chapter says performance support is stronger when it happens closer to the work.
explanation.direct: Static annual-review logic is weaker than continuous conversation and feedback.
explanation.competitive: A delayed verdict is weaker than live guidance.

questions.prompt: A student council leadership team wants stronger performance support through more regular check-ins, feedback, and recognition. What chapter logic does this reflect?
choices: The Part 2 shift toward continuous performance management and CFRs
A move away from all standards and accountability
The belief that goals alone can do all the management work

explanation.gentle: The chapter says performance improves when support becomes more ongoing.
explanation.direct: CFR-like practices help carry the work between formal goal-setting moments.
explanation.competitive: The system gets stronger when the support stays alive between targets.

questions.prompt: Which misreading does Chapter 15 warn against?
choices: Continuous performance management means constant surveillance or judgment theater
CFRs involve conversation, feedback, and recognition
OKRs work inside a broader performance system

explanation.gentle: The chapter says ongoing management is not the same as endless pressure.
explanation.direct: Continuous support is stronger than static review without becoming constant surveillance.
explanation.competitive: If your answer is nonstop judgment, you missed the chapter.

questions.prompt: Why do OKRs need a broader performance system in Part 2?
choices: Because goals need ongoing conversation, feedback, and recognition to support performance over time
Because goals stop mattering once the system appears
Because the chapter says performance should no longer be discussed

explanation.gentle: The chapter says goals are stronger when the surrounding support system is stronger.
explanation.direct: OKRs define direction, but CFRs help sustain and improve the work continuously.
explanation.competitive: Goals point the work. The system keeps it moving.

questions.prompt: A tutoring program staff wants better performance support without turning the program into nonstop pressure. Which response best fits the chapter?
choices: Build useful ongoing conversation, feedback, and recognition instead of relying only on periodic judgment
Keep all support inside one annual formal review
Increase the amount of judgment without improving the quality of conversation

explanation.gentle: The chapter wants a steadier support system, not constant pressure.
explanation.direct: Continuous management is stronger when it improves conversation and feedback rather than just multiplying judgments.
explanation.competitive: More pressure is weaker than better signals.

questions.prompt: What deeper point does Chapter 15 make about OKRs and CFRs?
choices: They belong together because goals need a continuous support system around performance
They belong in separate management worlds
They matter mainly because the acronyms sound modern

explanation.gentle: The chapter joins goals with the conversations and feedback that help people carry them over time.
explanation.direct: OKRs and CFRs form a stronger system together than either one does alone.
explanation.competitive: A target without a live support system is strategically thinner.

Because CFRs replace the need for company stories
Because Adobe appears before the Part 2 transition in the book
